A trigonometry explainer · with opinions

Circles All the Way Down

One circle, one triangle, and everything they secretly run. Drag the point. Then let a PID controller chase it and explain the observable universe. Then watch us model a square out of circles, because apparently modeling is hard. Then pull on a block, slowly, and catch friction being electromagnetism the whole time. Finally, put a gas under a piston and watch it run its own PID loop — with a sidebar on the thirteen-ish numbers that made the gas possible. Then assert P, I, and D inside each molecule, start them all one Planck length apart, and see what the crowd decides. Then ask how far a runner should lean, and get an answer smaller than anyone wanted. Then meet the professors who made all of it feel possible — Larry and Chau, Dr. Yuan, John, Roseanna, Balaji — and, last, Hari, who draws a cube and derives the rest.

The wave below is just the point’s height, plotted against time.

The triangle was inside the circle all along

Take a circle of radius 1. Put a point on it at angle θ. Drop a line straight down. You now own a right triangle whose hypotenuse is exactly 1 — which means the two legs stop being “opposite over hypotenuse” homework and become plain coordinates: the horizontal leg is cos θ, the vertical leg is sin θ. Pythagoras collapses into sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, which is just the circle saying “radius is 1” in algebra.

tan is a slope, not a ritual

tan θ = sin θ / cos θ = rise over run — the slope of the radius line. That’s why it explodes near 90°: the line goes vertical and slope stops being a number. Nothing mystical happened; you divided by a cos that went to zero.

Waves are circles seen from the side

Let the point travel at constant speed and write down its height over time: that’s a sine wave. Its shadow’s position over time: cosine. Every oscillation you’ll ever meet — pendulums, alternating current, a plucked string, tides — is some circle you’re watching edge-on. Keep that picture and the identities stop being flash cards.

The entire theory, in one sentence

A PID controller computes how wrong you are — the error — and pushes back with three terms: P reacts to how wrong you are right now, I to how long you’ve been wrong, and D to how fast the wrongness is changing. Present, past, future. Weight them, sum them, push. That is the whole theory, and it quietly runs most of the built world — and, once you see it, most of the unbuilt one.

Try the presets: pure P arrives with drama and oscillates forever. Crank Ki and the integral hoards old grievances until it overshoots spectacularly — that’s windup. Too much Kd flinches at everything. “Tuned” is what competence feels like: boring.

Everything, explained

P · delayed

Hotel showers

You are a proportional controller acting on 8-second-old water temperature. Scald, freeze, scald: a textbook limit cycle. The shower is fine. Your loop delay is not.

PD

Standing upright

Your inner ear runs PD control on your ankles a few dozen times a second. Alcohol adds latency and lowers Kd. Ever seen someone whose balance oscillates? Ever seen them try to add D by holding a wall?

PID

Cruise control

Not a metaphor. It is literally this demo with a hill instead of a circle. The I term is what holds speed on the grade; without it you'd crest every hill 6 mph sad.

I · windup

Deadlines

Small error, small effort — for weeks. The integral of “slightly behind” accumulates silently, then discharges as one saturated all-nighter. Procrastination is unmanaged integral windup.

I · 18-mo lag

Central banks

Integral control on inflation with an actuator that takes a year and a half to do anything. Overshoot isn’t a risk; it’s the spec sheet.

D · excessive

Group chats

Nobody responds to the message. Everyone responds to the trend of the messages. A community of pure-D controllers with no setpoint: maximum reactivity, zero steady state.

P · bang-bang

Thermostats

Technically bang-bang control — PID for people who gave up. Your furnace is either furious or dead, which may also describe the group chat above.

I · geological

Evolution

No P, no D — just an integral term with a four-billion-year horizon, slowly zeroing out the error between creature and habitat. Occasionally it winds up. We call those mass extinctions.

A square wave — nature’s least circular object — built from rotating circles alone.

“Modeling is hard” — people who haven’t tried circles

You hear it constantly: reality is messy, nonlinear, high-dimensional, fundamentally resistant to mathematics. Compelling. Anyway, here is a square — jagged, discontinuous, aggressively un-round — emerging from a handful of circles spinning at odd multiples of one frequency. Fourier showed in 1807 that essentially any periodic signal surrenders to this treatment. Every sound you have ever heard reached your brain as a sum of sines. So technically, nothing has been hard since 1807.

The little horns at each corner are the Gibbs phenomenon. They never fully go away no matter how many circles you add. Ignore them. Everyone does.

Field notes from the practice

  • The standard method. Step 1: assume a spherical cow. Step 2: the sphere is just a circle with delusions of grandeur. Step 3: circles are solved, see tab 01. The cow is now trigonometry.
  • On nonlinearity. Linearize about the operating point, then refuse — as a matter of principle — to ever leave the operating point.
  • Calibration (n.) The art of turning knobs until the model agrees with the data you already had. Not to be confused with prediction, which is calibration against data you don’t have yet, and is traditionally someone else’s problem.
  • Precedent. Ptolemy modeled the entire visible sky with circles on circles. He was wrong for 1,400 years — but confidently, quantitatively, publishably wrong, which for most purposes is indistinguishable from right.
  • On validation. All models are wrong. Some are useful. Mine converged, which is a third thing that impresses people at meetings.
  • On steady state. Assume steady state. Nothing is steady. Assume it anyway. The transient is just the model being shy.
  • If model and reality disagree. Ship the model. Reality has no version control and refuses to document its assumptions.

Q: Why does an object pulled slowly pull back harder?

Because friction isn’t a fundamental force. There are four of those, and friction didn’t make the list — it’s electromagnetism with a body count. Zoom in on any two “touching” surfaces and they actually meet at a few microscopic peaks; the true contact area is a tiny fraction of what your eyes report. At those junctions the atoms’ electron clouds get close enough to bond — van der Waals attraction, and in clean metals outright cold welding (two metals in vacuum will simply decide to be one metal). Every junction is a little electromagnetic spring.

Now pull slowly. The junctions have time. Under pressure the contact peaks creep, flatten, and grow — more real contact, more bonds, and older, better-settled bonds that hold to a higher stretch before they break. You aren’t fighting a “static friction coefficient”; you’re fighting a construction project that has been running since the surfaces met, and your slowness is its budget. Pull for longer, pull back harder.

Yank instead, and the bonds die young. Each junction snaps before it has had time to settle, and the fresh ones forming behind it are weaker newborns — so the sliding resistance stays low. That’s the entire secret behind static > kinetic friction, and behind the sawtooth in the chart above: force builds while bonds age, snaps in a cascade, builds again. A squeaky door hinge, a violin bow catching a string, chalk shrieking on a blackboard, and most earthquakes are that exact plot at different sizes. (A fault that has been “pulled slowly” for 300 years has had 300 years to strengthen. This is not reassuring, but it is trigonometry-adjacent.)

You have never touched anything

While we’re here: the normal force is the same story from the other axis. Push the surfaces together and the electron clouds refuse to overlap further — electromagnetic repulsion plus the Pauli exclusion principle, which is less a force than a firmly worded policy. You are hovering a fraction of a nanometer above your chair right now, electromagnetically levitated. “Contact” is a macroscopic rumor. Two of Newton’s favorite forces, friction and normal, are the same force measured along different axes of the same handshake — which is, of course, a cos and a sin of the same underlying thing. Tab 01 sends its regards.

House position: this is excellent news for the rest of the tool. The bonds are springs; springs oscillate; oscillations are circles. And stick-slip is what happens when nature runs pure P control against a plant that strengthens while you hesitate — tab 02 has the sliders, tab 03 has the apology for how easy this all was to model.

Le Chatelier was describing a controller

Perturb a gas and it pushes back in proportion to how far you pushed — that’s P, and its name in the gas is pressure. Push it fast and it pushes back harder than the displacement alone would justify — that’s D, and its name in the gas is viscosity. Hold it perturbed and let the walls talk to the outside world, and a slow term accumulates until the last bit of offset is gone — that’s I, and its name in the gas is heat. No one installed this loop. It falls out of 110 dots bouncing, or 10²³ in your tire, with no additional assumptions. Tab 02, wearing a cylinder.

TermIn the gasWhere it comes fromWhat it fixes
PPressureBoyle: pV = NkT, so a squeezed gas pushes back in proportion. The spring constant is K_p = γp/V — the bulk modulus.Position, fast — with overshoot.
DViscosityStress ∝ rate: μ = ⅓ ρ v̄ λ. Resists fast motion, ignores slow. Independent of density — Maxwell found this so implausible he verified it in his attic in 1866. Weak in a dilute gas, which is why the piston rings a while and why dashpots are filled with oil, not air.Overshoot — eventually.
IHeat exchangeNewton’s cooling: dQ/dt = h·(T_res − T). Accumulates until the adiabatic-vs-isothermal offset is gone. The second law is an integrator.Steady-state error, slowly.
SetpointThe loadMechanical equilibrium: p·W = F. Add a weight and you’ve issued a step input.Where “correct” is.
Noise√NPressure is an average over collisions. Here N = 110, so about ±10%. In a tire N ≈ 10²³, so ±10⁻¹¹.Why the ideal gas law looks like a law: it has 10²³ votes.

What to try

+ Weight is a step input. Watch the piston overshoot, ring, and settle — the same curve as “Tuned” in tab 02, except nobody tuned it. With thermal contact at zero the cylinder is adiabatic: the piston settles at the adiabatic height, visibly above the isothermal one, because compressing the gas heated it and the heat has nowhere to go. That gap is steady-state error, exactly what a P-D controller leaves behind when Ki = 0.

Now slide thermal contact up. Molecules that hit the walls are re-drawn from the reservoir temperature; heat leaks out; the piston sinks toward the isothermal line. That drift is the integral term finishing the job — and notice it is slow, the way I terms are slow, because it moves at the rate of heat, not the rate of pressure. Yank the piston and you’re watching D: the gas objects to the rate, not just the position.

Pressure is a statistic

The pressure readout jitters because it is not a property, it is a poll: the momentum delivered to the piston by whichever molecules happened to arrive in the last quarter second. With 110 voters the margin of error is about 10%. With Avogadro’s number of voters it is 10⁻¹¹, which is the difference between “a statistic” and “a law.” Every thermodynamic quantity is like this — temperature, entropy, the works — a mean over chaos, presented with a straight face. The gas doesn’t have a pressure; it has a habit.

Fine print: this is a two-dimensional gas, so γ = 2 and the adiabat is T·V = const rather than T·V^⅔. The piston is adiabatic; only the walls talk to the reservoir. Boltzmann’s constant is 1 throughout, which is a choice of units, not a simplification — see the sidebar. And if pV/NkT creeps above 1 under heavy load, that isn’t a bug: the molecules have a size, and at high compression their own area starts to count. Van der Waals called it b. The guide lines assume he didn’t exist.

The ≈13 numbers that define reality

Dimensionless, so they don’t depend on anyone’s choice of ruler. Change one and the gas above stops being possible.

α≈ 1/137.036

Fine-structure constant — the strength of electromagnetism. Sets atom size, all of chemistry, and how hard the molecules above bounce. Tab 04, as a single number.

mₑ/mₚ≈ 1/1836

Why nuclei sit still while electrons do the chemistry. Sets molecular stiffness, the speed of sound, and why a gas has a temperature you can define at all.

α_G = Gmₚ²/ħc≈ 5.9×10⁻³⁹

Gravity’s weakness relative to electromagnetism. Why stars can exist and why this cylinder is not a black hole.

α_s≈ 0.118

Strong coupling. Nuclei hold together. Shift it ~10% either way and there is no carbon, or no hydrogen.

ε0.007

Fraction of mass released fusing hydrogen to helium. At 0.006 deuterium never forms and stars don’t light; at 0.008 no hydrogen survives to make gas.

G_F·mₚ²≈ 1.0×10⁻⁵

Weak coupling. Sets how slowly the Sun burns and how supernovae eject the elements. Neutrinos’ entire personality.

v/M_Pl≈ 2×10⁻¹⁷

The Higgs field’s value in Planck units — the hierarchy problem stated as a number. Why particles have masses so absurdly far below the scale where gravity matters.

η≈ 6.1×10⁻¹⁰

Baryon-to-photon ratio: how much matter survived annihilating with antimatter. Everything you see is the rounding error.

Q≈ 2×10⁻⁵

Amplitude of primordial density ripples. Smaller: no galaxies condense. Larger: only black holes do.

Ω1.000 ± 0.002

Total density parameter — flatness. The expansion rate that neither recollapses nor empties out.

Ω_Λ≈ 0.685

Dark energy’s share today. In Planck units the cosmological constant is ~10⁻¹²², the most embarrassingly small nonzero number in physics.

D3

Spatial dimensions. Stable orbits and inverse-square laws only work here. In four, atoms fall apart; in two, there are no knots and no digestion.

θ_QCD< 10⁻¹⁰

Strong CP phase. Allowed to be anything from 0 to 2π. Is zero. Nobody knows why. Enter the axion.

“Thirteen-ish” because the count depends on who’s counting: Rees says six, the Standard Model plus ΛCDM say about thirty. Note what is not here — c, ħ, G, kB. Those aren’t facts about reality, they’re exchange rates between units. Set them all to 1 and nothing happens except your textbooks get shorter; the gas above runs with kB = 1 and has not complained.

Three molecules, one contact law

Tab 05 let a PID loop emerge from dumb molecules. This tab does the opposite: it asserts the loop inside each molecule and asks what the crowd does. Every blob here is a soft disk, and when two overlap by δ the contact pushes back with F = k·δ + c·δ̇ + k_I·∫δ dt — P, D, I, on the overlap. A P blob carries only the spring; a D blob adds the damper; an I blob adds the integral. Mixed contacts average the two parties’ constants. This isn’t a metaphor: the spring-plus-dashpot half is exactly the linear contact model of the discrete element method (Cundall & Strack, 1979), the workhorse of granular mechanics. Your P-D molecule is a legitimate grain of sand.

Each species has a thermodynamic personality. P conserves energy — Newton-approved, the gas is simply a gas. D loses energy on every collision (restitution ≈ 0.6 here), and a gas of them does something spectacular: it collapses. Dense patches collide more, cool faster, get denser — the clustering instability of granular gases (Goldhirsch & Zanetti, 1993). Set D to 100%, warm-start, and watch the temperature chart fall off a cliff while the blobs freeze into clumps.

The I molecule is a small crime

The integral term is faithful to the loop and unfaithful to physics. Because ∫δ dt keeps growing through the whole contact, the push during separation exceeds the push during approach, so every collision does net positive work. I blobs manufacture energy out of contact time. A gas of them boils without a heat source; it is active matter, a swarm of tiny engines. Which means the composition sliders are a thermostat: I pumps, D drains, and the mixture finds the temperature where the two agree. The gas’s temperature becomes a policy decision. Open the valve and the box’s composition chases the inflow ratios with a residence-time lag — an integral controlling the integrals.

One Planck length apart

Big Bang places every blob on a lattice with spacing ℓP and zero velocity: the entire population inside one contact, every spring at full compression, and then release. That is inflation, as implemented by a spring-dashpot. Two honest footnotes. First, the Planck length in these units is about 10⁻³⁵, and a double-precision number near 0.7 cannot represent anything smaller than ~10⁻¹⁶, so the lattice spacing actually used is 10⁻⁹ — still a ten-millionth of a molecular radius; the difference is unobservable, which is the most Planck-length thing about it. When two blobs sit closer than the arithmetic can resolve, the contact takes its direction from the lattice ordering instead — the sub-resolution structure that decides which way things fly. In the real universe that job belongs to Q ≈ 2×10⁻⁵ in the sidebar of tab 05. Second, the explosion needs a speed limit: faster than c = 2r / 2Δt a blob would tunnel through its neighbor between timesteps, which is rude. So this universe has a c = 6, and the readout counts collisions that hit it. It is not relativity. It is the Courant condition wearing a cape.

Fine print: contact stiffness is set so a collision lasts about 25 timesteps; the integral resets when a contact ends; a contact can push but never pull (no cohesion), so the I term cannot make blobs stick. The outlet only opens while the valve is on — otherwise a sealed box, and P blobs conserve energy to the decimal.

The lean you feel and the lean that exists

Here is the calculator’s finding, before the fine print: at a steady pace, the whole-body lean the physics requires is between a fifth of a degree and about two degrees, for everyone, at every distance pace. It is set by one thing — air resistance — through one triangle: tan θ = F_drag / (m·g). Gravity is the adjacent side. Drag is the opposite. Tab 01 sends its regards. Lean more than that at constant speed and one of two things must happen: you accelerate, or you fall. There is no third option in which the extra lean is quietly converted into speed, because momentum can’t be converted into speed — momentum is speed, wearing a mass.

What the lean actually does at steady pace is line up the average ground-reaction force through your center of mass, so that over a stride the horizontal impulses sum to zero and you neither pitch forward nor tip back. That is the whole job. Which is why the acceleration slider is there: the moment you want to speed up, the required lean becomes atan((a + F_drag/m) / g), and a sprinter clearing the blocks at roughly 1 g is leaning roughly 45° — not as a style, as a consequence.

Then where does the forward feeling come from?

Two real places, neither of them momentum. First, trunk inclination: good runners carry the torso 5–10° ahead of vertical, and the evidence for it is orthopedic rather than propulsive — a few degrees of trunk flexion shifts load from the knee toward the hip and reduces patellofemoral stress (Teng & Powers, 2014). It is a joint-loading choice, and it does not move the whole-body line, because the hips and legs sit behind it to compensate. Second, the stance falling angle: while one foot is planted, your center of mass sweeps forward over it, so at toe-off your body is genuinely tilted 20–30° ahead of the support foot. That is the angle Pose-method coaches call “falling,” and it is real — but it is geometry of the stance phase, set by how far you travel during ground contact divided by leg length, not a posture you choose. It changes with pace, which the chart shows, and which is probably the lean you were thinking of.

Letting your legs catch up

This part is not a metaphor either. Each leg gets one swing time — from its toe-off to its next touchdown — to get back around in front of you, and that time shrinks as pace rises. Weyand and colleagues (2000, 2010) found the fastest humans reposition a limb in about 0.35 s and that this floor, together with how much force you can hit the ground with in an ever-shorter contact, is what caps top speed. Not lean. The “fastest leg swing” slider is yours to set; the calculator solves for the speed at which your swing time would run out, which is the mechanical ceiling your legs — not your posture — impose. Above it, no angle helps. You would simply be falling with style.

Where gender goes

Not into the lean, and for a clean reason: centre-of-mass height cancels out of the torque balance, because drag and gravity both act at the centre of mass, so tan θ = F_drag / (m·g) contains no length at all. But mass distribution is real, and it enters two other places. First, the stance falling angle is atan(x / h_CoM), and on population averages women carry the centre of mass about two percent of stature lower (≈ 0.55 H against 0.57 H), which is worth roughly a degree at toe-off — that is the slider above, and the selector sets its default. Second, the rotational momentum: the swinging legs carry angular momentum about the vertical axis and the arms swing to cancel it (Hinrichs, 1987). That momentum scales with the lower-body share of mass, which also differs by sex on average, so it changes how much arm and trunk counter-rotation a run costs — a quantifiable distinction, but one that lives perpendicular to lean. Drag needs a frontal area (Du Bois, 1916; scaled to running posture after Pugh, 1971) and stance needs a leg length; neither has a gender term. The selector fills in typical height, weight, and centre-of-mass height, and then steps aside.

Model notes: contact length and cadence are empirical fits to treadmill data across 3–10 m/s (contact time ≈ 0.25 s at 5:00/km, ≈ 0.11 s at 10 m/s; cadence 175 → 245 spm), scaled by leg length. Frontal area ≈ 0.24 × BSA, Cd ≈ 0.9, sea-level air. Drag’s share of running cost uses ~4 J·kg⁻¹·m⁻¹ and 25% muscular efficiency, which reduces neatly to Fdrag/m. Touchdown and toe-off angles are the foot-to-centre-of-mass line measured from vertical, splitting the contact length 40/60 — landing a little ahead of the hips, leaving well behind them. Everything here is a population-average model; your own stance and swing are yours to measure.

Money in the bank

In 2011 Larry Silverberg and Chau Tran — with an undergraduate named Taylor Adams — ran more than a million three-dimensional basketball trajectories to ask a question every playground has an opinion about: when should you use the glass? The answer had a shape. From the wings, between the free-throw lane and the three-point line and out to about twelve feet, the bank shot is roughly twenty percent more likely to go in than the same shot aimed straight at the rim. Straight on, and from farther out, aim at the iron. The reason is geometric: the backboard turns a small target into a big one, because a ball that hits the board a little high or a little low still comes off toward the same rim, and the friction of backspin against the glass takes speed off the ball and drops it in.

The second finding is the useful one. The best aim points on the board form a V near the top of the painted square — higher and farther from the rim as you move away from the lane, lower and closer as you move in — and all of them line up on a single vertical line standing 3.327 inches behind the backboard. Aim where that line appears to cross the V from where you stand and the physics does the rest. The panel above computes the same thing the paper did, live: for your spot it searches release angle, speed, and aim, bounces the ball off the glass with restitution and spin friction, and then shakes the release a few hundred times to estimate how often it drops.

How to swing

Larry’s other lesson is a playground swing, because it is the friendliest example of parametric resonance there is. You don’t push a swing from the inside; you change its length. Stand up as you pass the bottom — where the swing is moving fastest — and you raise your center of mass against the largest centripetal load, doing work on the pendulum. Sit down at the ends, where you are momentarily still and it costs nothing. Two pumps per period, and the amplitude grows a little every cycle. Stand at the wrong moment and you are a brake. The slider lets you get it wrong on purpose.

Larry sold exotic birds before he taught mechanical engineering and, eventually, before he took on a stray aerospace Park Scholar as a mentee. Every tab in this tool is a descendant of the way he and Chau Tran taught dynamics: draw it, then make it answer to numbers.

A wing that moves itself

The senior design brief was bio-inspired flight, and Dr. Fuh-Gwo Yuan steered the group toward the hardest thing a bird does casually: landing on a branch. A perching bird flares to an absurd angle of attack, sheds a wake of vortices, uses the drag to kill its speed in a wingspan or two, and folds. To do that with a machine you need a wing that changes shape without hinges and motors, which is where Yuan’s enthusiasm lived. A macro fiber composite is NASA Langley’s answer to the fact that piezoelectric ceramics are brittle: slice the ceramic into fibers, lay them in epoxy between interdigitated electrodes, and the sheet becomes a flexible patch that strains about 1800 parts per million along the fibers at +1500 V. Bond it to one side of a thin beam and the beam curves — the panel computes the unimorph curvature exactly, and it is enough to move the tip of a 20 cm cantilever by three and a half centimeters. Drive it with alternating voltage near the first bending mode and a modest patch flaps the whole wing.

The other actuator was NiTiNOL muscle wire: a nickel–titanium alloy that remembers a shape. Cold, it is martensite and stretches easily; run a current through it and above about 70 °C it transforms to austenite and pulls back four percent of its length with real force. The catch is hysteresis — it lets go at a lower temperature than it grabbed at — so the loop in the panel is the wire’s whole personality, and a controller has to live inside it. Wire it to a horn and it swings a flap; wire several across a wing and the wing reconfigures into the M that lets a perching bird stall gracefully instead of falling.

Taylor already suspected aerospace was not his direction by then. The wing got built anyway — fibers, wire, custom fabrication, and a professor who could not stop being interested. That is what these tabs are for.

Does the thumb change the flow, or just the speed?

Both — and the order matters. Cover part of the outlet and the jet visibly speeds up, which is the part everyone knows. What the riddle is really asking is where the extra speed came from. Write the energy balance from the spigot to the open air: the pressure head at the tap is spent on two things, friction along the hose and the kinetic energy of the jet, and the friction term scales with the velocity in the hose squared. Squeeze the outlet and the total resistance rises, so the flow rate drops; less flow means less velocity in the hose, less friction, and the pressure that friction was eating is freed to become jet speed. The thumb does not add energy. It reallocates it, from heat in the hose to speed at the nozzle. Set the hose length to zero in the console and watch the trick fail: with no friction to reclaim, the jet speed is pinned at √(2gH) — Torricelli — and covering the outlet only cuts the flow. The thumb works because of friction.

How coral gets away with it

Broadcast-spawning corals release sperm and eggs into moving water and hope. The classical accounting says that hope is misplaced: each cloud dilutes as it spreads, the encounter rate goes like the product of two concentrations, and the product of two diluted clouds is vanishingly small — models predicted efficiencies far too low to sustain a reef. Reefs exist. John Crimaldi built a flume with a two-dye laser-induced-fluorescence rig, released the two dyes as stand-ins for the gametes, and watched what turbulence actually does before it mixes: coherent eddies stretch each cloud into filaments and fold filaments from the two sources against each other, so for a while there are places where both concentrations are high at once. The encounter rate depends on the mean of the product, not the product of the means, and the difference between those — the covariance — is where the reef lives.

The flume above is a cartoon of that experiment: two dyes, a mean current, a slider’s worth of eddies, and both bookkeepings running live. Turn the stirring to zero and the covariance vanishes with it.

Roseanna and the sewer map

Eight subdivisions, a few sampling points downstream, a signal in the wastewater. Which neighbourhood has the outbreak? Run the plume backwards.

Running the plume backwards

The forward problem is the easy one: put a pulse into subdivision 5, let advection carry it down the laterals and trunks while dispersion smears it out, and predict what each monitor sees, when. Roseanna Neupauer’s question was the inverse: you have the monitors’ time series and you want the source. You could run the forward model once per suspect and compare — eight subdivisions, eight runs, and a thousand if it were a city. The adjoint method turns that around. The same advection–dispersion equation, run backward in time from the monitor with the sensor as its source, gives the probability that a particle detected there came from any location upstream — every candidate at once, one run per sensor. Neupauer and Wilson first wrote it for aquifers; the same reciprocity makes it work in pipes, and it was extended to distribution networks with imperfect sensors and non-detects.

The panel reframes her classroom example for wastewater epidemiology. Each subdivision sheds into a lateral; laterals join trunks; trunks pass sampling manholes and reach the plant. A hidden neighbourhood has an outbreak and sends a pulse. As the hours of samples accumulate, the backward probability — shaded on the map — tightens on the source. Watch what matters: a monitor that sees nothing is evidence too, and the timing of the peak, not just its height, is what separates a near source from a far one. That is dispersion doing the fingerprinting.

The transport here is a one-dimensional advection–dispersion travel-time distribution per path (inverse-Gaussian, mean Σ L/u, variance Σ 2DL/u³), the sensors are Gaussian-noisy, the unknown mass is fitted by least squares, and the prior over subdivisions is flat. Real networks have transients, incomplete mixing at junctions, and decaying signals; the shape of the argument survives all of them.

Mark them, let them go, count again

Balaji taught the hypergeometric distribution with a pond. Net some fish, tag every one, release them. Come back, net again, and count how many of this catch already wear a tag. If the pond holds N fish and M are tagged, the number of tagged fish in a net of n follows the hypergeometric: P(k) = C(M,k)·C(N−M,n−k) / C(N,n). You know M, n, and k; the only thing you don’t know is N, so turn the formula around and ask which N makes your catch least surprising. The rough answer is the Lincoln–Petersen estimate N ≈ Mn/k; the careful answer is the whole likelihood curve, which is what the panel draws, and which narrows with every cast you write down. That was the lesson inside the lesson: keep careful notes, because each cast is a factor in the likelihood and the notebook is the model.

Tunneling through the hills

When the Hill Tunneling Optimization work needed a critic and the original advisor said it wasn’t in their wheelhouse, Balaji read it and asked the questions that mattered. The idea is simple to draw: descend to a local minimum, then, instead of climbing out, solve for another point at the same height on the far side of the ridge — tunnel — and descend again. The critique is the statistician’s: what is the stopping rule, how do you know the tunnel found the deepest basin rather than the nearest one, and how does it compare against the dumbest honest competitor, a handful of random restarts? Press Tunnel and watch both the idea and the questions.

Hypergeometric likelihoods are computed exactly in log space; the credible interval is the central 95% of the posterior under a flat prior over N. The tunneling sketch scans outward from the current minimum for the first point below it, then descends by gradient — a cartoon of Levy–Montalvo tunneling, not the algorithm.

Everything comes from the cube

The trick, as Hari taught it, is to refuse to memorize the Navier-Stokes equations and instead memorize one picture: a small box of fluid with sides dx dy dz. Count what crosses its faces and you have conservation of mass. Add up the pushes on its faces — pressure normal to them, viscous drag along them — and gravity through its middle, set that equal to mass times acceleration, and you have conservation of momentum. That is the whole of Navier-Stokes: Newton’s second law, per cubic metre, for something that flows. The equation looks fearsome only because the acceleration of a parcel of fluid has two parts — it can speed up in place (∂u/∂t) or be carried into a place where the flow is faster (u·∇u) — and the second part is nonlinear, which is where all the trouble and all the weather lives.

The second trick is that you almost never solve the whole thing. You put your numbers in — a length, a speed, a fluid — and ask which terms are big. Inertia goes like ρU²/L, viscosity like μU/L²; their ratio is the Reynolds number, and it tells you which term to cross out. Gravity against inertia is the Froude number and tells you whether the free surface can stay flat. Hari would cross out terms on the board with real satisfaction, and what remained was usually something you could solve before lunch: Stokes flow in a pore, which averages up into Darcy’s law; the Euler equations in the middle of a reservoir; hydrostatics almost everywhere. The equation you actually use is the one the cube leaves behind.

For Harihar Rajaram, who drew the cube from memory and made the rest of us believe we could too.
